title: Spotlight: Staff Update on Outreach Activities Related to the Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Audits and Financial Reporting
author: PCAOB Staff

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The PCAOB outreach supports the cluster’s core proposition: current GenAI deployment is narrow and uneven, firms expect augmentation rather than wholesale replacement, and useful adoption depends on human review, continuing accountability, controls and training. Its findings are reported firm practices and expectations rather than independent performance evidence, so they corroborate rather than materially extend the synthesis.

kp.k: Findings reflect limited outreach, not binding regulatory policy
kp.d: The July 2024 Spotlight reports PCAOB staff observations from limited outreach to several audit firms and companies, rather than a representative quantitative study. Participating audit firms included U.S. global network firms and several U.S. non-affiliated firms auditing more than 100 issuers; collectively, they audit the majority of issuer market capitalization. Observations concern auditing and financial reporting, not legal services, and reflect practices at the time of outreach.

kp.k: Current audit adoption concentrates on administration and research
kp.d: Staff characterize integration as early-stage and rapidly evolving. Interviewed firms primarily used GenAI for administrative documents, initial drafts of audit-related memos and presentations, and research into internal accounting and auditing guidance. Global network firms were generally further along in developing and deploying tools than non-affiliated firms.

kp.k: Firms anticipate broader audit applications while continuing investment
kp.d: Most interviewed firms reported continuing investment in internally developed or third-party-supported GenAI tools. Potential future applications included summarizing accounting policies and legal documents, checking audit documentation completeness, risk assessment, audit scoping, checking disclosure completeness, and comparing financial statement figures with audited amounts. These were prospective uses, not findings that such tasks had already been successfully automated.

kp.d: Interviewed firms did not currently view PCAOB auditing standards as obstacles to developing and using GenAI in audits. Separately, PCAOB staff described a research project assessing whether technology-based tools warrant guidance, standards changes, or other regulatory action; the Spotlight itself announces no such change.

kp.k: Human responsibility persists under an augmentation model
kp.d: Firms investing in GenAI expected it to augment rather than replace people in auditing and financial reporting. Some said existing supervision and review policies remained unchanged: engagement team members retained responsibility for results and documentation, and supervisors were expected to exercise the same diligence as for work completed without GenAI. These are reported expectations and policies, not measured employment outcomes.

kp.k: Auditability requires checking sources and generated content
kp.d: Some audit firms emphasized auditability of both source data and generated content, with some designing tools to document underlying sources. Reported risks included false or misleading outputs, bias, and incomplete or compromised source data. Some firms were developing more specific instructions or queries to improve response consistency and accuracy; the document provides no measured error rates or demonstrated mitigation effects.

kp.d: Firms emphasized policies, procedures, internal controls, and staff training, sometimes treating GenAI governance similarly to governance of other technologies. Identifying and assessing emerging risks remained a reported priority.

kp.k: Financial reporting adoption trails operational and customer-facing uses
kp.d: Staff reported that preparers were exploring GenAI across their businesses, with accounting and financial reporting integration appearing secondary to operational and customer-facing integration. Reported financial reporting uses included drafting internal accounting summaries and presentations, comparing company information with public competitor information, and assisting with relatively simple repetitive processes such as account reconciliations and identifying reconciling items.

Some were testing individual use cases to determine the controls required before wider integration, rather than assuming existing controls were sufficient.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source describes early GenAI adoption in auditing and financial reporting, potential expansion into substantive work, and continuing requirements for human review and governance.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source: its claims concern auditing and financial reporting, not legal services. PCAOB staff report that current audit use among the firms interviewed is primarily administrative and research-oriented, including initial drafts of memos and presentations and research into internal accounting and auditing guidance. Staff report that global network firms are further along in development and deployment than non-affiliated firms. Most interviewed firms report continued investment and foresee possible assistance with summarizing accounting policies and legal documents, checking audit documentation and financial statement disclosure completeness, risk assessment, audit scoping, and comparing financial statement amounts with audited amounts. Interviewed firms do not currently view PCAOB standards as impediments. Firms investing in GenAI expect augmentation rather than replacement of humans; engagement team members remain responsible for work and documentation, and supervisors retain their review responsibilities. Some firms restrict or prohibit use in audit or attest procedures because of privacy and reliability risks. Interviewees identify potentially false, misleading or biased output, incomplete or compromised input data, and amplification of existing information technology risks or creation of new ones. For financial statement preparers, staff report that accounting and reporting adoption is secondary to operational and customer-facing adoption. Some preparers report drafting internal documents and assisting with repetitive work such as reconciliations. Preparers foresee efficiency improvements but emphasize human supervision, output review, controls and governance. They identify inconsistent output and opaque tools as obstacles to auditability, and possible difficulties controlling training-data quality for third-party models.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of limited qualitative outreach and interviewees’ reports of practices, risks and expectations, not measured performance or demonstrated productivity gains.
pts.d: PCAOB staff conducted outreach in the months preceding the July 2024 publication, mainly with larger audit firms and representatives of several financial statement preparers. The audit-firm group comprised U.S. global network firms and several U.S. non-affiliated firms auditing more than 100 issuers; collectively, they audit the majority of issuer market capitalization. Current-use observations rest on participants’ accounts, while future applications, efficiency benefits and human augmentation are expectations expressed by participants. The document supplies no quantitative adoption estimates, controlled comparisons, productivity measurements, model benchmarks or measured hallucination rates. It distinguishes staff views from Board rules, policy or statements. Its discussion of possible regulatory action describes an ongoing research project assessing whether guidance, standards changes or other action are needed, rather than announcing a regulatory change.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings are a July 2024 snapshot of early, evolving adoption; broader audit applications and efficiency improvements are conditional possibilities without a specified delivery date.
pts.d: Staff characterize integration as early-stage and rapidly evolving, and restrict their observations to uses discussed at the time of outreach. Descriptions are qualified by terms such as some firms, most firms interviewed and some preparers, rather than asserted for the entire profession. Proposed substantive audit applications are future possibilities, not established capabilities or universal deployments. Broader integration depends on addressing confidentiality, security, output reliability, source-data auditability, human review and internal controls. Some firms currently prohibit GenAI in audit or attest procedures. Some preparers are testing individual use cases to establish necessary controls before wider financial reporting integration. Statements that standards are not impediments describe the interviewed firms’ current views, not a guarantee about future regulation. The source gives no deadline for widespread adoption or replacement of particular tasks.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct subjects are large audit firms, their engagement teams and supervisors, and companies preparing financial statements; the report anticipates changed workflows rather than quantified workforce displacement.
pts.d: Audit staff gain assistance with drafting and guidance research, with possible future assistance in planning and performing audits. Engagement team members retain responsibility for results and documentation, and supervisors remain responsible for diligent review of AI-assisted work. Global network firms are described as ahead of non-affiliated firms in developing and deploying tools. Financial statement preparers use or explore GenAI in drafting, reconciliations and other reporting processes, while prioritizing operational and customer-facing applications. Companies under audit face confidentiality concerns when their information is uploaded into tools. Firm and company governance functions must address policies, training, controls, data reliability and technology risks. PCAOB staff are researching implications for audit quality and possible regulatory responses. The source does not predict specific headcount reductions, fee changes, legal-market effects or measured benefits to investors.
